lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you dissolved salt in water. Is salty water a new substance? No: it is a mixture, and you can get the salt back.
A mixture is two or more substances mixed but not joined: air, sea water, muddy water and ink. Each keeps its own properties, so we can use them to separate it.
A substance that dissolves is soluble; one that will not is insoluble. Salt (the solute) dissolves in water (the solvent) to make a solution.

Filtering separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The filter paper's tiny holes let water through but trap the sand. The solid left behind is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
Evaporating gets a dissolved solid back. Warm salty water in an evaporating basin: the water turns into vapour and leaves, and salt crystals stay behind.
Distilling gets the pure liquid back. Boil the salty water; the steam cools in a condenser and drips out as pure water. Some dry countries make drinking water from sea water like this.

Chromatography separates the colours in an ink. Put a dot of ink on a pencil line on paper and dip the edge in water. Each dye travels up at its own speed. A pure substance makes one spot; a mixture makes more.
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, draw a felt-tip dot above a pencil line on kitchen paper. Dip the edge in water and watch the colours split. Next: solids, liquids and gases.

exercises.prompt: Which method separates sand from water?
exercises.hint: Sand does not dissolve: which method traps a solid but lets a liquid through?
exercises.explain: Filtering: the paper traps the sand and the water runs through.

exercises.prompt: Match each method to what it separates.
matches: a solid that did not dissolve
exercises.hint: Think about what each method keeps at the end.
exercises.explain: Filtering keeps a solid that did not dissolve; evaporating gets a dissolved solid back; distilling gets the pure liquid back; chromatography splits the dyes.

exercises.hint: Is it one substance, or water with salts dissolved in it?
exercises.explain: True: sea water is water with salts and other substances mixed in.

exercises.prompt: Sort the substances: soluble or insoluble in water?
exercises.hint: Picture stirring each into water: does it disappear, or sink to the bottom?
exercises.explain: Soluble: salt, sugar and instant coffee. Insoluble: sand, chalk and pebbles.

exercises.prompt: What is the solid left in the filter paper called?
exercises.hint: The filtrate is what passes through; the other word is for what stays.
exercises.explain: The residue stays in the paper; the filtrate passes through it.

exercises.prompt: Dissolving salt in water makes a new substance.
exercises.hint: Can you get the salt back by evaporating the water?
exercises.explain: False: the salt is still salt. Evaporating gets it back, so no new substance was made.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to get pure salt from rock salt (salt mixed with sand).
exercises.hint: First dissolve the salt, then remove what will not dissolve, then get the salt back.
exercises.explain: Crush it, dissolve the salt in water, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to leave salt crystals.

exercises.hint: Follow the liquid: heated in the flask, cooled in the tube, collected in the beaker.
exercises.explain: The heat boils the liquid in the flask, the thermometer reads the steam's temperature, the condenser cools it, and the distillate drips into the beaker.

exercises.prompt: How many dyes are in the black ink?
exercises.hint: Count the separate spots in its column: each spot is one dye.
exercises.explain: The black ink splits into 3 spots, so it is a mixture of 3 dyes.

exercises.hint: A pure substance makes just one spot.
exercises.explain: Ink A makes one spot; inks B and C split into two dyes each.

exercises.prompt: Which method gives drinkable water from sea water?
exercises.hint: The salt is dissolved: which method collects the pure liquid?
exercises.explain: Distilling: the water boils off and condenses pure, leaving the salt behind. A filter lets dissolved salt through.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a mixture or a pure substance?
exercises.hint: Is it one substance all the way through, or several mixed together?
exercises.explain: Mixtures: air, sea water and orange juice. Pure substances: pure water, oxygen and gold.

exercises.prompt: In chromatography the start line is drawn in pencil, not in ink.
exercises.hint: What would happen to an ink line when the water reached it?
exercises.explain: True: pencil does not dissolve, so the line stays put. An ink line would run up the paper too.

exercises.prompt: Why can a filter not get the salt out of salty water?
choices: Dissolved salt slips through the holes.
exercises.hint: Think how small the salt's particles are once it has dissolved.
exercises.explain: Once dissolved, the salt is spread out as tiny particles that pass through the filter with the water.

exercises.prompt: A dye travelled 3 cm up the paper while the water travelled 6 cm. What is its Rf value (the dye's distance ÷ the water's distance)?
exercises.hint: Divide how far the dye went by how far the water went.
exercises.explain: 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5. The same dye always has the same Rf value on the same paper and solvent.

exercises.prompt: Which dyes are in the mix?
exercises.hint: A dye in the mix makes a spot at the same height as that dye on its own.
exercises.explain: The mix's spots are level with the yellow and the blue dyes, not with the red one.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when you distil salty water.
items: Pure water drips into the beaker
The steam cools in the condenser
exercises.hint: Follow the water from the flask to the beaker.
exercises.explain: It is heated, it boils into steam, the steam condenses back into water in the condenser, and pure water drips out. The salt stays in the flask.

exercises.prompt: Match each job to the best method.
exercises.hint: Ask what each method keeps: a solid, a dissolved solid, a liquid, iron, or the big pieces.
exercises.explain: Muddy water: filtering. Salt: evaporating. Pure water: distilling. Iron filings: a magnet. Pebbles: a sieve.

exercises.prompt: Evaporating salty water gets back the water as well as the salt.
exercises.hint: Where does the water go when it evaporates from an open basin?
exercises.explain: False: the water escapes into the air as vapour. To keep the water too, you must distil it.
